1.blurb: The Abbasid Caliphate in Baghdad at the time of the first Viking raids was heir to a millennium of Persian imperial administration. The Abbasids had taken power from the Umayyads in 750 on the strength of Persian and Khurasani support, and their court culture, bureaucratic practice, and intellectual life were deeply Persian. The dirhams the Vikings would chase across the Volga were minted in a city built on Persian models by a dynasty running a Persian-staffed government.

The Carolingian Empire that the Vikings would soon begin raiding was built on top of the old Celtic Gaul. Julius Caesar's conquest of Gaul in the previous century had absorbed the Celtic heartland into Rome, and Roman Gaul became Frankish Gaul, then Carolingian France. The people the Vikings raided in Francia were heirs of the same Celtic-Roman-Germanic world that had produced the druids and the torcs.

While Viking longships were beaching on the coast of Northumbria, the Byzantine Empire was tearing itself apart over religious images — the decades-long Iconoclast controversy over whether icons were holy art or forbidden idols. The empire that shielded Europe's eastern flank was spending its energy smashing its own paintings.

At the other end of Eurasia the Tang dynasty, the most cosmopolitan empire on earth a generation earlier, was in its long decline after the catastrophic An Lushan Rebellion. The court still ruled from Chang'an, but provincial warlords were carving out autonomy the way Scandinavian chieftains carved out fjords.

In Japan the court had just moved to a brand-new capital, Heian-kyo (modern Kyoto), opening the Heian period — four centuries of aristocratic poetry and court ritual run by the Fujiwara family. While Norse warriors swore oaths in smoky longhouses, Heian nobles ranked each other by the elegance of their handwriting.

Across the Atlantic the Maya city-states of the Yucatán were at the dazzling height of their Classic period — towering pyramids, divine kings, and a written script no European would read for another thousand years. Within a century many of these cities would be mysteriously abandoned, just as the Viking Age was hitting its stride.

Meanwhile in early-medieval Europe: the North Sea was already a busy commercial highway, ringed by the wic trading towns — Hamwic, Lundenwic, Ipswich — that tied England to Frisian and Frankish ports. The same waters the Vikings would treat as an open road were a shared trade zone before they turned it into a war zone.

Meanwhile in the Islamic world: Damascus had been the Umayyad capital before the Abbasids moved the center of gravity east to Baghdad. By the Viking Age it sat inside the vast Islamic trade network whose silver dirhams would flow up the Russian rivers into Scandinavia.

Meanwhile in pre-Viking Scandinavia: the Vendel Age (c. 550–790) was the aristocratic, boat-grave society that produced the warrior culture, the ring-swords, and the seafaring skill the Vikings inherited — the dress rehearsal for the raids.

Meanwhile in pre-Viking Scandinavia: Vendel, in Uppland, gives its name to the era and to the spectacular boat-grave cemeteries (alongside Valsgärde) where the rowed, sailless clinker hull that preceded the longship was buried with its dead chieftains.

Meanwhile in Mesoamerica: the Maya Classic period was the golden age of the southern lowland city-states — Tikal, Calakmul, Palenque — at the very moment the first longships were beaching at Lindisfarne, a connected world neither half knew about.

2.blurb: Lindisfarne monastery, raided in 793, was itself the product of the Irish-Celtic Christian tradition. It had been founded in 635 by the Irish monk Aidan, trained at Iona — the same monastery the Vikings would raid two years later. The illuminated manuscripts the Vikings plundered were made by monks working in the Insular style, a fusion of Celtic animal-interlace art and Christian Latin scholarship. The Vikings didn't just raid a monastery; they raided the physical archive of Celtic Christian culture.

The Carolingian Empire the Vikings found so easy to raid was the political heir of Rome — Charlemagne had been crowned Holy Roman Emperor in 800, explicitly claiming the Roman imperial title. The land empire with heavy cavalry and no navy that failed to stop Viking longships was the same military model the Romans had used to dominate the Mediterranean. Viking longships exposed the fatal gap in Roman-derived land power: there was no answer to fast shallow-draft seaborne raiders in a world built for infantry and siege.

The Book of Kells is the supreme artifact of Insular Celtic Christian art — produced on Iona around 800, then evacuated to Kells in Ireland when Viking raids made the island too dangerous. Its survival is a direct consequence of Viking pressure; its existence is a product of the Irish-Celtic monastic tradition that Vikings spent the 9th century systematically raiding. The book is now in Trinity College Dublin, which means the Vikings inadvertently moved it to its permanent home.

As the Great Heathen Army carved up England, China's Tang dynasty was sliding toward collapse. The Huang Chao Rebellion (874) would gut the dynasty's heartland the way Norse armies were gutting Anglo-Saxon kingdoms — both empires undone by mobile forces the central state couldn't pin down.

While Saxon kings died in the Northumbrian rain, Baghdad was the intellectual capital of the world. At the House of Wisdom, scholars were translating Aristotle and Euclid into Arabic and doing original mathematics — the Abbasid golden age running at full power exactly as western Europe paid Vikings to go away.

In Japan the Fujiwara family had locked down the Heian court, ruling through child emperors and marriage politics while producing an exquisite aristocratic culture. A world away from the longship economy: power here was won with poetry and genealogy, not plunder.

Across the Atlantic the great Maya cities of the southern lowlands were being abandoned one by one — the Terminal Classic collapse, a civilization-scale unraveling whose causes are still argued. The Viking Age was beginning just as the Classic Maya world was ending.

The Oseberg ship burial — two high-status women interred in a decorated ship with sacrificial attendants and extraordinary grave goods — echoes the Scythian kurgan burials of the Pontic steppe a millennium earlier. Both traditions buried elite individuals with their possessions, sacrificial animals, and sometimes human companions. Ship burials and kurgan burials are the two great Iron Age traditions of taking your wealth with you into death, and they appear to reflect a shared steppe-and-northern-European understanding of what the afterlife required.

2.matchText: The genuinely terrifying escalation of the 840s
2.blurb: The same 840s decade that sent Norse fleets up the Seine to sack Paris also saw the Uyghur Khaganate destroyed by a Yenisei Kirghiz invasion, and the Carolingian empire formally fractured at Verdun. The Uyghur Steppe chapter on this decade — the eastern axis of that decade's cascade of collapses — shows how a world-spanning set of crises unfolded simultaneously at opposite ends of Eurasia.

Meanwhile in early-medieval Europe: the North Sea was the trade artery linking England's wic towns to Frisian and Frankish ports. The Vikings turned a commercial highway into a raiding corridor — and the boats vanished back into it as fast as they had come.

Meanwhile in early-medieval Europe: the Frankish realm under Charlemagne and his heirs was the great land empire of the West — heavy cavalry, monastic learning, no navy. Built to withstand a siege, it had no answer to a shallow-draft fleet that could be gone in three weeks.

Meanwhile in Anglo-Saxon England: the Northumbrian golden age that produced Lindisfarne, Bede, and Alcuin — the literate Christian world whose horror at the raids gives us so much of the written record of the Viking Age.
Meanwhile in pre-Viking Scandinavia: the Vendel Age (c. 550–790) was the boat-grave, ring-sword warrior society that bred the raiders — the world the men who beached at Lindisfarne came out of.

Meanwhile in pre-Viking Scandinavia: still a pagan patchwork of petty kingdoms and chieftain halls when Ansgar arrived to plant the first church — the homeland the raiding fleets sailed from and returned to each autumn.

Meanwhile in the Islamic world: the Umayyads had ruled the first Arab caliphate from Damascus before the Abbasid revolution; a surviving Umayyad prince fled to Iberia and founded the emirate of Córdoba, the Muslim power whose coast Hastein's fleet would raid.

Meanwhile in the Umayyad world: Spain was conquered in 711, and after the Abbasid takeover the lone surviving Umayyad rebuilt his dynasty at Córdoba — the Iberian power whose coast a Norse fleet raided on its way into the Mediterranean in 859.

Meanwhile in Byzantium: the Eastern Roman Empire still treated the Mediterranean as its own sea, alongside the Arabs — until a Norse fleet sailed in through Gibraltar and proved otherwise. The Rus' would soon be hammering on Constantinople's own gates (Chapter 4).

Meanwhile in the Islamic world: Baghdad was the Abbasid capital and the intellectual capital of the planet — its scholars translating Aristotle into Arabic while Saxon kings died in the rain. Its silver dirhams flooded north into Scandinavia for two centuries.

Meanwhile, the legacy of classical Greece: Aristotle's works, lost to the Latin West, survived through Arabic translation in Baghdad — proof that the ninth-century world was a single connected library even as its halves barely knew each other.

3.blurb: Iceland's Althing, founded in 930, was a parliamentary assembly that ran for 330 years on customary law and the authority of the Lawspeaker, with no king, no standing army, and no taxation. The Roman Republic, founded around 509 BCE, lasted nearly five centuries before being swallowed by one-man rule. The Icelanders had reinvented, independently, a republican form of governance in the North Atlantic — and lasted longer relative to population than most ancient experiments in collective self-rule.

Thorfinn Karlsefni's failed colony at Vinland around 1010 is one of the great near-misses of world history. At the same time Norse settlers were fighting the Skraelings in Newfoundland and retreating, Polynesian voyagers were completing their settlement of New Zealand — the last major uninhabited landmass on earth. Both peoples reached the limits of what pre-industrial population numbers and technology could sustain in a new environment. The Polynesians held New Zealand. The Norse could not hold Newfoundland.

Iceland's Althing and its Grágás law code — government by assembly and recited law, with no king — is the closest medieval analogue to the early Roman Republic's instinct that power must be plural and answerable, not vested in one ruler.
Meanwhile in Anglo-Saxon England: the patchwork of English kingdoms the Great Heathen Army was busy dismantling on the eve of the Viking storm.
Meanwhile in Anglo-Saxon England: the kingdoms whose survival hung on Alfred's stand at Edington.
Meanwhile in the Germanic world: the ancestral tongues whose northern and continental branches gave English its Germanic backbone.
Meanwhile in early-medieval Europe: the North Sea world the Viking raids stitched together — and tore apart.
Meanwhile in ancient Rome: Latin, the language that spread with Roman power and erased older tongues like Etruscan.

4.blurb: The Abbasid silver dirhams that Norse merchants collected in huge quantities on the Volga came ultimately from silver mines in Khurasan and Central Asia — the same Iranian plateau region that had been the economic heartland of the Persian empire for a thousand years. The Buyid dynasty ruling Baghdad in the late 10th century were themselves Iranian, keeping the Abbasid caliph as a figurehead. Persian imperial infrastructure, mining, and trade networks created the silver hoard that bankrolled the Viking Age.

The Varangian Guard served the Byzantine emperors in Constantinople — a city that sat at the intersection of the Greek East and the Persian-influenced Islamic world. Byzantine court culture, diplomatic protocol, and fiscal administration were all shaped by centuries of Persian influence; the Greek fire that burned Igor's fleet in 941 was a technology developed in a city whose intellectual tradition was deeply Hellenistic-Persian. Norse warriors in Constantinople were, at one remove, working for an institution that owed its administrative DNA partly to the Persian imperial tradition.

The Norse Rus trade routes through the Russian river system overlapped with territory the Scythians had controlled a thousand years earlier. The Pontic steppe north of the Black Sea — through which the Dnieper route ran — had been Scythian homeland from roughly 700 to 300 BCE. Norse traders portaging longships across the same watersheds that Scythian horsemen had commanded were, unknowingly, following corridors that steppe merchants and warriors had used for centuries.

4.matchText: political crystallization of the Rus' begins in the 860s
4.blurb: Meanwhile, told from the Rus' side: the Kievan Rus' narrative gives the full account of the Rurik story and the bitter Normanist controversy it feeds — including the hard external evidence that predates the Primary Chronicle's tidy 862 date, the 839 entry in the Annals of Saint-Bertin recording 'Rhos' envoys at the Frankish court who turned out to be Swedes. It also traces the assimilation mechanism by which a few thousand Norse warriors were demographically swallowed by a Slavic-speaking majority within three generations.

4.matchText: moved the Rus' political center south from Novgorod
4.blurb: Why Kyiv and not Novgorod? The Kievan Rus' narrative spells out the commercial logic this chapter compresses into two sentences: Kyiv was the choke point on the route from the Varangians to the Greeks, the hinge of the poliudye tribute circuit, and the place from which East Slavic tribute could be redirected from Khazar to Rurikid control. Oleg's seizure of the town was a strategic capture of the whole southern river economy, not just a change of address.

4.matchText: took the regency for their young son
4.blurb: The pigeon-fire revenge is the famous part; the consequential part is what came after. Told from the Rus' side, Olga's reign produced the first systematic state administration of Rus': she reformed the tribute system, fixing the poliudye rates and setting up the pogosty (collection stations) so that tribute became a predictable institution rather than a raiding expedition that could get a prince killed, as it had killed Igor. The saga of revenge frames a real administrative revolution.

4.matchText: the emperor's personal household troops, recruited overwhelmingly from Scandinavia
4.blurb: The Guard's founding cohort was the military half of a bargain. Told from the Rus' side, the 6,000 warriors Vladimir sent Basil II were the price of the emperor's sister Anna and of the conversion of 988 — and Vladimir had to besiege the Byzantine city of Chersonesus to force Basil to deliver the bride even after the troops had already shipped out. The Varangian Guard was a direct institutional product of that coerced Rus'-Byzantine treaty.

What happened to this Norse-founded trading state after Harald Hardrada's era? Told from the Rus' side: Yaroslav the Wise's rota succession system — the lestvitsa, where the throne rotated among brothers rather than passing father to son — turned out to be a machine for producing civil war, and the resulting fragmentation eventually broke the unified Rus' polity that had supplied the Guard's eastern recruiting pipeline. The structural cause of the collapse was a succession rule, not an invasion.

The silver and slaves the Rus' funneled south arrived in a Constantinople at its medieval height — the Macedonian Renaissance, a Byzantine flowering of art, scholarship, and reconquest. The Norse rivermen were feeding the richest court in Christendom.

The dirhams flowing up the Russian rivers were minted in a Persian world where the Shia Buyids held Baghdad and kept the Abbasid caliph as a figurehead — the political reality behind the silver that paid for Viking longships.

Much of the silver reached Scandinavia from Samanid Central Asia, where Bukhara rivaled Baghdad as a center of Persian letters. The Viking economy was plugged into a Eurasian system most Norse never saw.
As Norse traders worked the rivers, the Maya world was passing through its Postclassic transition — the old southern cities gone, new powers like Chichen Itza rising in the Yucatán.
Meanwhile in the Islamic Golden Age: the Baghdad-centered caliphate whose silver dirhams flowed north up the Volga to bankroll the Viking world.
Meanwhile in the Islamic Golden Age: Baghdad, the wealthiest city on earth, whose minted silver became the Norse trade economy's lifeblood.
Meanwhile in the Islamic Golden Age: the Abbasid mints that struck the tens of millions of dirhams the Rus' rowed home.
Meanwhile in the Islamic Golden Age: the dirham flood — the trade and silver economy that pulled Norse merchants down the Russian rivers.
Meanwhile in the Islamic Golden Age: the Caliphate's silver mining, trade revenues, and monetary policy that made the dirham flood possible.
Meanwhile in the early Caliphate: the Islamic state whose conquests and wealth set up the silver-rich world the Rus' traded into.
Meanwhile in Persia: the Sasanian empire whose silver coinage circulated alongside Abbasid dirhams in the Norse hoards.
Meanwhile in early-medieval Europe: the Frankish realm whose Danegelds paid off Viking raiders in the west.
Meanwhile in the Islamic west: Cordoba, where some of the slaves shipped down the Volga route ended their journey.
Meanwhile in Byzantium: the triple land walls that turned back every besieger of Constantinople, the Rus' included.
Meanwhile in Persia: the Sasanian state that shaped the Byzantine and Islamic worlds the Rus' did business with.
Meanwhile in the future: the Ottomans, who would finally take Constantinople in 1453 and dissolve the Varangian Guard.
Meanwhile in Anglo-Saxon England: a later recruiting ground for the Varangian Guard after 1066 sent English exiles east.

5.blurb: Norse mythology's central preoccupation with doomed heroism — fighting knowing you will lose at Ragnarök — has a structural parallel in the Scythian warrior ethos as described by Herodotus: warriors who preferred death in battle to dishonor, who dragged their enemies into suicide pacts, and who built the great kurgans as monuments to fallen chiefs. Both cultures built their warrior identity around the acceptance of inevitable death and the conviction that how you died mattered more than whether you survived.

Iceland's peaceful parliamentary conversion to Christianity in 1000 CE is worth contrasting with the violent Christianization happening elsewhere. The Phoenicians had faced the opposite pressure a millennium earlier — their Canaanite religious tradition being absorbed and eventually suppressed by the spread of monotheism from their Israelite neighbors. In both cases, an Atlantic-facing maritime culture was navigating the transition between older polytheist practice and a new universal religion. Iceland managed it without martyrs. The Phoenicians did not get the choice.

Olaf Tryggvason's forced Christianization of Norway echoed, in reverse, the Roman suppression of druidism in Britain and Gaul. The Romans had used military force to destroy the druidic sacred sites at Anglesey in 60 CE and ban the druid orders as a matter of state policy. Four centuries later, Olaf was doing the same thing to Norse paganism — destroying temples, killing recalcitrant pagan chieftains, and threatening mutilation for refusal to baptize. The mechanics of top-down religious suppression were identical across the centuries.

The Norse conversion window coincides with the founding of Song China (960) — soon the wealthiest, most administratively sophisticated state on earth, as Scandinavia was only just acquiring writing and territorial kingship.

While Norse kings were being baptized for diplomatic respectability, the Shia Fatimid Caliphate ruled Cairo at the height of its power — one of three rival caliphates in an Islamic world far richer and more urban than Christian Europe.
In Persia the Buyids still ran Baghdad behind a puppet caliph — the eastern political backdrop to the same generation that Christianized the north.
Meanwhile in Rome: Latin was the language of the empire and, after Constantine, of the western Church — the tongue that displaced runes for serious writing once the Norse converted.
Meanwhile among the Germani: the Norse gods belonged to a wider Germanic pagan family, with cousins worshipped by the continental tribes Rome first met centuries earlier.
Meanwhile in England: the Saxons who crossed to Britain were close kin of the Norse, sharing gods, language roots, and the same pagan-to-Christian arc.
Meanwhile in England: the cult of Saint Olaf spread as far as the Anglo-Saxon church, echoing how England had made its own martyr-king cults a generation earlier.
Meanwhile before the Vikings: the gods and cult sites converted away here had taken shape in the Vendel-era Scandinavia of the centuries just before the raids began.
Meanwhile in Francia: Frankish missionaries like Ansgar had been seeding Christianity into Denmark for a century, part of the wider Christianizing of the post-Roman West.
Meanwhile in Francia: the Holy Roman Empire pressuring Denmark to convert was the German-led successor to the empire Charlemagne had built.
Meanwhile in Germany: the empire that leaned on Harald to convert under Otto I would, a century on, be locked in the great struggle of pope versus emperor.
Meanwhile in the East: the same generation that converted the Norse saw the Buyids running Baghdad, the Abbasid capital at the heart of the Islamic Golden Age.

6.blurb: Ferdowsi's Shahnameh, completed around 1010, is roughly contemporary with the Norse Eddic poems reaching their likely composition. The Shahnameh is a 60,000-couplet epic of Persian royal history and mythology, composed in New Persian to preserve Iranian cultural identity against Arabic cultural dominance. The Norse Eddic poems preserved Norse mythology against Christian assimilation. Both traditions were acts of cultural conservation — a civilization's mythology written down at the moment of its transition to a new religious and literary order.

The Arabic literary flowering of the Abbasid court in the 9th and 10th centuries — translating Greek philosophy, producing original science, poetry, and theology — was, in large part, a Persian cultural production. Persian scholars, translators, and administrators drove the Bayt al-Hikma (House of Wisdom) in Baghdad. The silver dirhams from this civilization funded Norse raids across Europe; the intellectual output of this civilization was being produced at the same moment Norse skalds were composing the densest court poetry in medieval Europe.

The Norse heroic poems preserved in the Codex Regius include the story of Atli — Attila the Hun — and his destruction of the Burgundian kingdom, the same events that produced the German Nibelungenlied. Attila's campaigns through Europe in the 440s CE had passed through and shattered the same Germanic world that would later produce the Norse. The Huns who terrified Roman Europe left their mark in Germanic legendary tradition, and those legends traveled north with the Germanic migrations to become Norse myth.

6.matchText: Tang and Song Chinese poetic traditions
6.blurb: While skalds memorized dense court verse, China was in the greatest age of its lyric poetry — Li Bai, Du Fu, later Su Shi — written, anthologized, and central to the examination elite. Two opposite media: Norse oral runic memory vs. Chinese literary canon.

The Abbasid court sustained an Arabic poetic golden age exactly as the Eddic poems were taking shape — both elite traditions, but one written into a vast scholarly civilization, the other carried in memory on the rim of Christendom.
Meanwhile in Rome: Latin was the learned language of Christendom, the script the Norse adopted only after conversion — which is why pre-Christian Scandinavia wrote in runes instead.
Meanwhile among the Germani: the runes and heroic legends the Norse preserved descended from a wider Germanic tradition shared with the continental tribes.
Meanwhile in Byzantium: the Miklagarðr of the runestones was Constantinople, the wealthiest city the Norse knew, where Swedish adventurers served in the imperial guard.
Meanwhile in Byzantium: the Berezan' runestone marks a Swede who died returning from a Byzantine expedition — the empire whose silver drew the eastern Norse south.
Meanwhile in the Islamic world: the runestones call it Serkland, the land of the Caliphate, whose silver dirhams flooded north along the Volga route.
Meanwhile in Baghdad: the Norse poetic flowering ran alongside the Arabic literary golden age of the Abbasid court, the high point of medieval Islamic letters.
Meanwhile before the Vikings: the runic script and ship-burial culture of these texts had been maturing through the Vendel age that preceded the raids.

7.blurb: The Han dynasty's heqin tribute system — silk, grain, gold, and imperial princesses sent north to buy off Xiongnu raids — is the exact structural parallel to English Danegeld payments. A wealthy settled agricultural state, unable to secure its entire frontier against fast-moving mobile raiders, pays tribute that the raiders take and then returns for more. Han China paid heqin for nearly seven decades before the system broke down. England paid Danegeld for about thirty years with the same result. The settled-state arithmetic of tribute is identical across a thousand years and five thousand miles.

Dublin as a slave-trading maritime hub parallels Carthage's role in the ancient Mediterranean almost exactly. Carthage ran slave markets fed by raid networks across North Africa, Iberia, and the western Mediterranean, selling captives into agricultural and domestic labor. Dublin ran slave markets fed by Viking raid networks across Britain, Ireland, and the Continent, selling captives into Icelandic farms and eastern Mediterranean markets via the Volga route. Different sea, different century, same fundamental model: a fortified port city as the pricing and distribution center for human beings captured in organized raiding.

The Khazar Khaganate that controlled the lower Volga trade route — and whose destruction by Svyatoslav in 968 redirected Norse commercial networks — was the last major steppe successor state in a lineage going back through the Huns to the Scythians. The Khazars controlled the same Pontic steppe that the Scythians had dominated a millennium earlier. When Svyatoslav destroyed Khazaria, he was ending the last remnant of the great Eurasian steppe commercial system that the Scythians had first organized.

As Cnut welded together a North Sea empire, Northern Song China was becoming the wealthiest single state on earth — a centralized, paper-money, civil-service civilization that makes Cnut's personal-union realm look like the improvisation it was.
The same decades saw the Seljuk Turks beginning their sweep across Persia and toward Anatolia — the steppe-to-empire trajectory playing out at the other end of the Norse trade world.
Fatimid Egypt was at the height of its power and wealth while Scandinavia was still consolidating its first real kingdoms — a reminder of how marginal the Viking world was in global terms.

The 'pay the raiders to leave' logic of Danegeld had a deep precedent: a thousand years earlier Han China had bought off the Xiongnu the same way, and learned the same lesson about what tribute does and doesn't buy.
Meanwhile in England: the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms whose crown the Danish kings were now fighting to seize.
Meanwhile on the Continent: the Frankish (Carolingian) realm whose royal annals recorded Hedeby and whose markets fed the Norse trade towns.
Meanwhile in Islamic Iberia: al-Andalus, home of the Andalusian merchant At-Tartushi, whose travelogue gives us one of the only outside descriptions of a Norse town.
Meanwhile in the Islamic world: the Abbasid Caliphate, whose silver dirhams flowed up the Volga and into Birka's graves.
Meanwhile in the eastern Mediterranean: the Byzantine Empire, terminus of the Volga route and a buyer in the Norse slave trade.
Meanwhile, centuries earlier: Phoenician Carthage ran Mediterranean slave hubs on the same fortified-port model that Dublin would later mirror.
Meanwhile, just before: Vendel-era Scandinavia, the pre-Viking world out of which these trading towns and kingdoms grew.
Meanwhile to the south: the Holy Roman Empire, the unified Christian neighbor whose pressure helped drive Scandinavian state formation.
Meanwhile, eleven centuries earlier in China: the Xiongnu confederation, whom the Han bought off with heqin tribute exactly as England bought off the Vikings with Danegeld.
Meanwhile in the east: Constantinople, the Byzantine capital where Norse warriors served in the Varangian Guard.
Meanwhile in England: the Anglo-Saxon (Saxon) realm whose arrows would later kill Harald Hardrada at Stamford Bridge.
Meanwhile in China: the Song dynasty, stabilizing after the Five Dynasties and on its way to becoming the wealthiest state on earth.
Meanwhile in the Near East: the early Seljuk Turks pushing across Persia and Anatolia.

8.blurb: William of Normandy, who conquered England in 1066, was the great-great-great-grandson of a Norse warlord — but by his own time he was thoroughly French-speaking and culturally Norman. The England he conquered had itself been shaped by centuries of Viking settlement in the Danelaw and Norse-Irish influence in the northwest. The Battle of Hastings was, in one reading, a contest between different branches of the same Norse diaspora — Rollo's assimilated descendants fighting Harold Godwinson's Danelaw-shaped kingdom — for possession of a country that had originally been Celtic.

The Varangian Guard finally dissolved when Constantinople fell to the Ottoman Turks in 1453 — the same event that ended Byzantine civilization as a going concern. The Ottoman empire was, in part, built on the ruins of the Seljuk Turkish state that had first broken Byzantine military power at Manzikert in 1071, five years after Stamford Bridge. Norse warriors who had served the Byzantines since 988 were defending a city whose fall would shift the political center of the Islamic world to a dynasty that itself owed much to Persian administrative and cultural tradition.

Yaroslav the Wise's Russkaya Pravda law code, his Saint Sophia Cathedral modeled on Hagia Sophia, and his dynastic marriages across Christian Europe placed Kievan Rus in 1050 as a peer of the western European kingdoms in the Roman-derived political order. The Norse warrior elite that had founded Kievan Rus had, within six generations, produced a Christian monarch building Roman-style basilicas, issuing written law codes, and marrying his daughters to the kings of France and Hungary. The longship had become a cathedral.

The year the Viking Age ended, Northern Song China was at its commercial and demographic peak — the contrast between the world the Vikings exited and the world's actual center of gravity could hardly be sharper.
Five years after Hastings, the Seljuks would shatter Byzantine power at Manzikert (1071), opening the road to the Crusades — the medieval world the Viking Age fed into.
Meanwhile in England: the Anglo-Saxon political class whose entire defending core was destroyed at Stamford Bridge and Hastings in 1066.
Meanwhile on the Continent: the Frankish kingdom whose king Charles the Simple granted Normandy to the Viking Rollo in 911.
Meanwhile in the east: Constantinople, where Harald Hardrada had served in the Varangian Guard before sailing to claim England.
Meanwhile in the Roman inheritance: Latin, the language of the Carmen de Hastingae Proelio and the clerical chronicles that recorded 1066.
Meanwhile in the eastern Mediterranean: the Byzantine Empire, from whom Norman warlords would take Sicily and southern Italy.
Meanwhile in Constantinople: Hagia Sophia, the great church on which Yaroslav the Wise modeled his Saint Sophia Cathedral in Kiev.
Meanwhile, for scale: the Roman Republic, which lasted longer than the entire 273-year Viking Age.
Meanwhile in China: the Tang dynasty, another empire that outlasted the whole span of the Viking Age.
Meanwhile in the Islamic world: Baghdad, the Abbasid capital that the Norse dirham-flow trade networks reached from the North Atlantic.
Meanwhile in the east: Kievan Rus', the state founded by Norse expansion and the direct ancestor of medieval Russia.
Meanwhile in the Islamic world: the Caliphate, the silver-rich market the Norse slave and trade networks ultimately fed.
Meanwhile across the world: the Indian Ocean, where the Chola dynasty was projecting naval power at the very moment the Vikings exited the stage.
